title: KV tailwind caching — economic hit-rate modeling, decay-ladder TTL, and staged rollback orchestration
creator: Priya Patel
description: Problem: Large production workloads are paying high per-token costs because ineffective KV/prefix caching combined with conservative TTLs leads to low effective hit-rate and unnecessary model invocations. Goal: produce an automated recommendation engine plus a safe apply/rollback orchestration that (1) models economic value of candidate cache keys and prefixes, (2) synthesizes decay-ladder TTL proposals, and (3) drives a staged canary + shadow apply with clear rollback triggers. This ticket covers design, prototype instrumentation, and a deployable runbook for staging -> canary -> ramp -> GA. The intent is to reduce token cost per request while keeping p95 latency and QA signal unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: Recommendation engine produces TTL proposals for at least 80% of active prefixes with estimated ROI and confidence score
Staged apply workflow can run shadow, 1%, 5%, 20% canaries and auto-rollback when defined thresholds breach
Lift experiment in staging shows >= 10% cost reduction in simulated traffic for one pilot service without latency regressions
Dashboard surfaces top 20 candidate keys, estimated cost delta, hit-rate lift, and confidence band
Playbook documents exact rollback thresholds and escalation path and is runbook-reviewed by SRE

rollout_plan: Phase 0 (shadow): apply TTL rules in shadow for 24-72h, compute projected cost delta and hit uplift; Phase 1 (micro-canary): 1% traffic for 2h; Phase 2 (small-canary): 5% traffic for 6h; Phase 3 (ramp): 20% for 24h; Phase 4 (GA): remaining traffic with 72h guarded observation. Automatic rollback triggers: (a) cache_hit_rate drops below expected by >5% absolute and produces >2% increase in model invocations; (b) p95 latency increases >10% above baseline for the service route; (c) error rate (5xx or model-fallback) increases by >1% absolute. Human-in-loop: SRE gets page if any trigger is observed plus automated pause and roll-forward block. All phases include preflight simulator and dry-run smoke tests.
telemetry_queries:
-- sample query: aggregate hits and cost by prefix
SELECT prefix, count(*) AS reqs, sum(case when kv_hit then 1 else 0 end) AS hits, avg(tokens) AS avg_tokens FROM inference.requests WHERE ts BETWEEN $__from AND $__to GROUP BY prefix ORDER BY reqs DESC LIMIT 500;

-- cost projection join tokens and model price
SELECT prefix, avg_tokens, hits, reqs, (reqs - hits) * avg_tokens * model_unit_price AS projected_token_cost_without_cache FROM (subquery) LIMIT 200;

test_plan: 1) Unit tests for Bayesian smoothing and decay-ladder TTL generator. 2) Integration: run recommendation engine against historical trace and validate projected cost delta matches replayed results within 10%. 3) Shadow traffic run in staging for 72h. 4) Canary with automated health checks; forced rollback test to verify runbook executes. 5) Post-GA A/B audit to validate live ROI after 7 days.
risks: Overaggressive TTLs may increase cold-miss behavior for bursty prefixes and cause model invocation spikes
Telemetry sampling bias — low-frequency prefixes may have unstable estimates leading to bad recommendations
Interference with other caching layers (edge CDN or app-level caches) — coordinate with platform and infra teams
Rollback automation false positives could lead to oscillation if thresholds poorly tuned
notes: Design choices and novel elements: (1) Decay-ladder TTL: per-prefix TTL expressed as a small discrete set of lifespans (e.g., [30s, 2m, 10m, 1h]) chosen to limit eviction churn and make behavior predictable for KV shards. (2) Economic hit-rate model: estimate ROI as avoided token cost minus additional memory/shard pressure cost; use a conservative prior to avoid recommending for low-sample prefixes. (3) Safe apply: combine shadow-run validation with micro-canaries and a hysteresis window to prevent oscillation. Trade-offs: we bias toward safety for P1 services while allowing P3 internal services to opt into aggressive mode.
